result:
There is a specific minute, just after the sun drops behind the ridgeline but before the sky fully commits to night, when the water holds a color that has no name. Not gold. Not grey. Something the eye invents on the spot, existing only in the act of looking, dissolving the moment you try to pin it down.

I stood at the edge of a lake in Vermont last October and watched that unnamed color stretch across two hundred yards of still water. The pines on the far shore had gone black. The sky peeled from bruise-purple at the horizon into a clean, indifferent blue. And the water in between was... I don't know. Something. A held breath.

What strikes me is the arrogance of naming. We file every flower into a Latin binomial. We catalog the stars into constellations that are just our need for story grafted onto indifference. And yet the water, in that single unrepeatable minute, asks us to simply witness. To let the color be color without a tag. To stand in the gap between what is and what we've decided to call it.

I think about that minute more often than I should. I think about it when I'm mid-sentence, searching for the word, and realize the word will flatten the thing into something smaller.

The color was really there. The color is gone. I am here, trying to write it back, which is, I suppose, the most human thing I know how to do.

"There is a specific minute, just after the sun has dropped behind the ridgeline but before the sky has fully committed to night, when the water holds a color that has no name. It is not gold. It is not grey. It is something the eye invents on the spot, a color that exists only in the act of looking, that dissolves the moment you try to pin it down in language.

I stood at the edge of a lake in Vermont last October and watched that unnamed color stretch across two hundred yards of still water. The pines on the far shore had already gone black. The sky above was doing its slow gradient work, peeling away in layers from the bruise-purple at the horizon up into a clean, indifferent blue. And the water in between was... I don't know. Something. A held breath.

What strikes me is the arrogance of naming. We walk into a meadow and file every flower into a Latin binomial. We catalog the stars into constellations that are just our need for story grafted onto indifference. And yet the water, in that single unrepeatable minute, asks us to simply witness. To let the color be color without a tag. To stand in the gap between what is and what we have decided to call it.

I think about that minute more often than I should. I think about it when I'm mid-sentence, searching for the word, and realize the word will flatten the thing into something smaller than what was actually there.

The color was there. The color is gone. I am here, trying to write it back, which is, I suppose, the most human thing I can do."
